children: By Jennifer Hiller

A tiny California startup founded earlier this year is taking the "Bring Your Own Power" trend that is dominating the AI race to a whole new level-it is relying on 3-D printing technology to help make backlogged power equipment.

Parallax, which was founded by a Stanford University graduate who previously co-founded a defense hardware company, has raised $117 million to enter the market for a key piece of equipment made by industrial giants: gas turbines.
The company aims to make smaller, gas-fired turbines designed specifically for on-site power for data centers, leaning on 3-D printing technology instead of the specialty supply chain for turbines.
The market for large turbines used at power plants has multiyear backlogs due to rising demand for power, much of it coming from the artificial intelligence boom.
Given long wait times to connect to the power grid, many data centers are deciding to go it alone and build their own power generation on site.
Large manufacturers such as Caterpillar and Cummins are pivoting their businesses to feed a booming market for once-prosaic power equipment. Elon Musk wants to make power-turbine components, too.
The details

Parallax founder and CEO Carl Schoeller said the idea isn't to attempt to replicate the highly efficient turbines that major manufacturers build for power plants and aircraft. Instead, he wants to make something smaller that could generate about 10 megawatts of electricity, be manufactured faster with cheaper materials and be transported in shipping containers.

Schoeller said a traditional gas turbine core has more than 2,000 parts, while Parallax's design would use 3-D printing to simplify manufacturing down to a handful of parts. The Parallax turbine would operate at lower combustion temperatures, which reduces fuel efficiency but allows the company to use more common materials and tap in to many broad supply chains, including those of the aerospace industry, he said.
"That's really our key differentiator," Schoeller said. "We don't have to design for a utility. We don't have to design for aircraft. We get to design for this customer."
With the recent fundraising, Parallax aims to build its first prototype by year-end, test it next year and deliver to customers in 2028, Schoeller said.
Many Parallax units would be needed at each data center site, as companies are looking for hundreds to thousands of megawatts of power.
The context

Data center developers and tech companies have been locking down power generation equipment, from turbines to reciprocating engines and fuel cells, as they race to connect data centers to electricity sources as quickly as possible.

Generac shares soared last week after it reached a long-term deal to supply generators to Amazon.com for its data centers. Generac said it expects initial deliveries of backup generators to total $2.4 billion in 2027 and 2028.
Musk has purchased a turbine manufacturer and said on X recently that SpaceX will start making the blades and vanes that go into natural-gas-fired power turbines.

Lior Susan, founder and chief executive of Eclipse, which invested in Parallax, said neither chip makers nor the power industry are adding enough capacity to meet the demands of AI data centers, which has left the market "starved."
"Building a gas turbine is freaking hard, but if you can do it well, naturally it can be a gigantic business," Susan said.

He compared Parallax's plans for "parts consolidation" with SpaceX's approach to the rocket engine. Other Parallax investors include Lux Capital, Founders Fund, Greylock Partners and General Catalyst.
